newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Four Serbs, one Croat freed after Western protest.
newsitem.headline: Four Serbs, one Croat freed after Western protest.

text.p: Four Serbs and a Croat jailed under murky circumstances by Bosnia's Moslem-led central government were freed after a protest letter by international peace officials, U.N. police said on Thursday.

The five were released from Sarajevo's main prison on Wednesday, said Jim Landale of the U.N. International Police Task Force (IPTF) monitoring law enforcement and human rights problems in post-war Bosnia.
Two of the Serbs, Sekula Mandic and Cedo Vukadin, vanished on July 2 while driving on a road south of Sarajevo that crosses alternating patches of Moslem and Serb-held territory.

The other Serbs, Radenko Golijanin and Predrag Matkovic, were snatched from their car on the same road on September 6 after it was ambushed by gunmen in civilian clothes, believed to be Moslem security police.
The Croat, Franjo Markovic, was a policeman who was arrested in a Sarajevo suburb early this week.

Landale said a letter protesting against the detentions was sent to the Bosnian government on Tuesday by Admiral Joseph Lopez, commander of NATO peace forces, civilian peace coordinator Carl Bildt and IPTF Commissioner Peter Fitzgerald.
"We followed these detentions very closely. We could get no clear answer as to the substance and nature of the alleged offences," Michael Maclay, a spokesman for Bildt, told Reuters.

"There were rumblings about 'war crimes' but they were so general we didn't get the answers we needed. So we made representations at the highest level quite discreetly and as result the people were freed."
Landale said Markovic was initially accused of unspecified war crimes, then of narcotics trafficking only, then of war crimes again "so it seems the (authorities) weren't quite sure."
None of the five was on a roster of 75 people indicted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal on former Yugoslavia.

To curb jailings on trumped-up, ethnically-motivated charges, mediators implementing the 1995 Dayton peace treaty secured commitments from Bosnia's factions last year to arrest for war crimes only those on the U.N. list.
